title: Python SDK: ergonomic event-adapter layer for streaming chat + retry semantics
creator: Aria Patel
description: Improve the Python SDK developer ergonomics for streaming chat completions by adding a lightweight event-adapter layer that normalizes event shapes, simplifies backpressure handling, and consolidates retry/cancellation semantics across sync and async APIs.
background: Users of the Python SDK currently use a combination of raw event streams (dicts) and multiple helper utilities in examples. This has led to inconsistent patterns across apps: ad-hoc parsing of 'delta' events, duplicated backoff/retry logic, and confusion when converting between async generators and synchronous iterator bridges. Recent customer feedback and internal examples show common anti-patterns (blocking reads on the event stream, poor partial-response retries, and leaky cancellation semantics).
problem_statement: We need a small, well-documented abstraction that: 1) emits typed events for the most common streaming shapes (response_chunk, tool_call, structured_output, error), 2) provides a consistent retry model for idempotent streaming requests and resumable KV-cache friendly requests, and 3) exposes easy-to-use sync wrappers for blocking code-paths without exposing implementation complexity.
proposed_solution: Add an 'EventAdapter' layer in the python SDK that sits between the raw transport and consumer callbacks/iterators. Key features: (a) a typed Event class enum + minimal attributes, (b) an AsyncEventIterator that yields Event objects and offers a .ack() API for backpressure controlling, (c) a SyncEventIterator adapter that safely runs the async iterator in a background thread and forwards cancellation signals, (d) pluggable RetryPolicy objects with presets (no-retry, fast-retry, resumable-kv-retry) and hooks into SDK-level idempotency tokens, (e) a small set of examples (contextmanager usage, middleware chaining) and tests covering race conditions and spurious reconnects.
design_decisions: 1) Event shapes: minimal and forward compatible — only provide 'type', 'payload', 'seq', 'meta' fields so we can add new event kinds without breaking. 2) Backpressure: use explicit .ack(bytes) where possible; for basic use we provide a 'auto_ack' mode. 3) Retries: separate concerns — transport reconnection vs. request-level retry. Resumable retry requires server support; when server does not advertise resume tokens fall back to full-request retry. 4) Sync bridge: use background thread plus a queue with configurable maxsize to avoid unbounded memory growth.
tradeoffs:
- Introduces a small API surface that we must support across versions; to mitigate we use a minimal core and mark advanced hooks as experimental.
- Sync bridge adds thread overhead for sync users; acceptable for common apps but documented as not for high-throughput pipelines.
- Resumable retry increases complexity (state + checkpointing) but yields large cost/latency wins for long sessions; default policy will be conservative.
benchmark_plan: Run end-to-end benchmark suite comparing current raw-stream patterns vs EventAdapter with: average latency per token, peak memory under high-concurrency (1000 concurrent streams), retry success rate under simulated network blips, and CPU impact of sync bridge threads. Record results in internal perf dashboard and include sample config used.
acceptance_criteria: EventAdapter implemented and exported from sdk.redwood.streams module
AsyncEventIterator yields typed events with documented ordering guarantees and includes an ack/backpressure API
SyncEventIterator provides a clear cancellation path and is covered by unit + integration tests
RetryPolicy presets implemented (no-retry, fast-retry, resumable-kv-retry) with unit tests for policy selection and backoff math
Examples added: context-manager streaming example, sync-bridge example, and migration guide for existing users
Benchmarks show no >10% median latency regression in simple chat generation, and memory remains bounded under concurrency tests
API docs and changelog entries added; PR reviewed and approved by SDK leads and one runtime engineer
